item.text:
I used the local prior as the structured baseline and did not use the client matrix. I also kept this to a source-family summary, not an 80-lens score pass.

**What Xi’s office looked like in 2022**
- Xi held the core CCP/state posts: General Secretary of the CPC, Chairman of the CPC Central Military Commission, President of the PRC, and Chairman of the PRC Central Military Commission.
- The party constitution gives the General Secretary power to convene the Politburo and its Standing Committee and to preside over the Secretariat.
- The CMC chair has overall responsibility for the armed forces.
- In October 2022, the 20th Party Congress and its first plenary session renewed Xi as General Secretary and CMC chair, with a new Standing Committee packed with loyalists.

**What constrained him in 2022**
- The main constraints were practical and political, not formal checks.
- The zero-COVID system generated rare street and campus protests in late November.
- The government then moved quickly to soften quarantine/testing rules in early December.
- Economic headwinds were already present by mid-2022: mobility restrictions, weak normalization, and slowing growth.
- Rights criticism, especially around Xinjiang, Hong Kong, censorship, and protest suppression, remained intense.

**Best source families**
- Official Chinese party/state texts for office, authority, and policy position.
- Reuters for independent event chronology and external framing.
- SIPRI for security and military context.
- World Bank and IMF for macro conditions.
- Amnesty Chinese for critical local-language human-rights narrative.

**Retained Sources**
1. [Full text of Constitution of the Communist Party of China](https://english.court.gov.cn/2022-10/27/c_824962.htm) - Supreme People's Court / CPC Constitution text, 2022-10-27.  
   Precise fact: the General Secretary convenes the Politburo and Standing Committee and presides over the Secretariat; the CMC chair has overall responsibility for the armed forces.  
   Period fit: formal authority stack in late 2022.  
   Ruler attribution: direct, institutional.  
   Limitations: party legal text, not a behavioral record.  
   Contrary points: it does not show informal bargaining or implementation friction.

2. [Xi Jinping's report to the 20th National Congress of the CPC](https://www.xinhuanet.com/politics/leaders/2022-10/25/c_1129079429.htm) - Xinhua, 2022-10-25.  
   Precise fact: Xi’s report frames the congress around modernization, national rejuvenation, and strategic consolidation.  
   Period fit: captures Xi’s 2022 agenda and narrative frame.  
   Ruler attribution: direct, but from official propaganda.  
   Limitations: rhetorical and self-justifying, not an audit.  
   Contrary points: late-2022 protests and the policy reversal show that implementation was less stable than the report suggests.

3. [20th CPC Central Committee First Plenary Session Communique](https://www.xinhuanet.com/politics/cpc20/2022-10/23/c_1129075992.htm?id=488112) - Xinhua, 2022-10-23.  
   Precise fact: Xi was elected General Secretary and CMC chair; the new Standing Committee was filled with loyalists.  
   Period fit: immediate post-congress consolidation.  
   Ruler attribution: direct.  
   Limitations: official communiqué only, no dissent or process detail.  
   Contrary points: Reuters treats this as a precedent-breaking third term and notes the absence of a successor.

4. [China's Xi clinches third term, packs leadership with loyalists](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/chinas-xi-clinches-third-term-packs-leadership-with-loyalists-2919033) - Reuters via Investing.com, 2022-10-23.  
   Precise fact: Xi secured a third leadership term and a loyalist top body.  
   Period fit: independent read on power consolidation in October 2022.  
   Ruler attribution: direct.  
   Limitations: wire framing, not a deep causal analysis.  
   Contrary points: official Chinese sources present the outcome as orderly party procedure and collective leadership.

5. [China tightens security after rare protests against COVID curbs](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/china-reports-another-daily-record-of-covid-cases-as-protests-ripple-across-china-2952419) - Reuters via Investing.com, 2022-11-27.  
   Precise fact: protests spread across cities and campuses; the dissent was unprecedented under Xi.  
   Period fit: major late-2022 constraint event.  
   Ruler attribution: indirect, but clearly a backlash against ruling policy.  
   Limitations: fast-moving protest reporting in a closed environment.  
   Contrary points: officials largely denied the unrest and framed controls as necessary public-health management.

6. [COVID-19 response further optimized with 10 new measures](https://english.www.gov.cn/statecouncil/ministries/202212/08/content_WS63913c92c6d0a757729e4135.html) - State Council / Xinhua, 2022-12-08.  
   Precise fact: the 10-point notice relaxed quarantine/testing and curbed arbitrary lockdown expansion.  
   Period fit: immediate post-protest policy shift.  
   Ruler attribution: direct state action under Xi’s system; personal attribution is inferential.  
   Limitations: official notice, no explicit causal link to protests.  
   Contrary points: it still described the move as optimization, not abandonment, of zero-COVID.

7. [World nuclear forces](https://www.sipri.org/yearbook/2023/07) - SIPRI Yearbook 2023, 2023.  
   Precise fact: China was in the middle of significant nuclear modernization and expansion; the stockpile was expected to keep growing.  
   Period fit: strategic baseline for 1B across 2022-2023.  
   Ruler attribution: indirect, state capability rather than personal conduct.  
   Limitations: open-source estimates, not Chinese official counts.  
   Contrary points: China’s declared no-first-use posture is not the same thing as stockpile growth.

8. [Trends in World Military Expenditure, 2022](https://www.sipri.org/publications/2023/sipri-fact-sheets/trends-world-military-expenditure-2022) - SIPRI, 2023-04-24.  
   Precise fact: China remained the world’s second-largest military spender in 2022, at roughly $292 billion.  
   Period fit: military burden and regional-security context for 2022.  
   Ruler attribution: indirect, state-level capacity.  
   Limitations: estimates, methodology and exchange-rate sensitivity.  
   Contrary points: spending level does not by itself prove aggressive intent or operational use.

9. [China Economic Update: Between Shocks and Stimulus](https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099640106102210762) - World Bank, 2022-06-01.  
   Precise fact: Omicron outbreaks and mobility restrictions disrupted normalization and the World Bank projected sharper 2022 slowdown.  
   Period fit: inherited economic conditions before the late-2022 policy reversal.  
   Ruler attribution: indirect, macro conditions rather than personal conduct.  
   Limitations: forecast-oriented and technocratic.  
   Contrary points: official Chinese statistical releases can differ somewhat and later revisions can move the numbers.

10. [People's Republic of China: 2022 Article IV Consultation](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2023/067/002.2023.issue-067-en.xml) - IMF, 2023-02-03.  
   Precise fact: growth slowed significantly in 2022; policy turned expansionary; weak productivity and SOE structure clouded medium-term prospects.  
   Period fit: retrospective macro assessment of Xi’s 2022 environment.  
   Ruler attribution: indirect, policy environment rather than personal rule.  
   Limitations: macro and institution-focused, not a political narrative.  
   Contrary points: Chinese authorities emphasize stability, targeted stimulus, and long-run strategy.

11. [2022年度中国人权报告](https://www.amnesty.org/zh-hans/latest/research/2023/03/anuual-report-22-china/) - Amnesty International 中文, 2023-03-28.  
   Precise fact: documents harsh COVID restrictions, censorship, arrests of critics, and continued repression in Xinjiang, Tibet, and Hong Kong; it also ties the November protest wave to the Urumqi fire and lockdown anger.  
   Period fit: strong narrative summary of 2022 rights conditions.  
   Ruler attribution: direct to the Xi system, though not every act is personally ordered.  
   Limitations: advocacy-based and example-driven.  
   Contrary points: official Chinese claims frame the same policies as public-health necessity and national-security management.

**Compact event map**
- October 2022: 20th Party Congress, Xi secures a third term, and the new top leadership is stacked with loyalists.
- Late October 2022: the congress report and party constitution formalize the governing frame and the center’s authority.
- November 2022: rare protests erupt over COVID controls after the Urumqi fire.
- December 7-8, 2022: Beijing softens zero-COVID controls with 10 new measures.
- Mid-2022 through year-end: macro conditions remain weak, with slowed growth and policy strain.
- All year: repression and censorship remain central, with Xinjiang and Hong Kong still major external-pressure points.

**Chapter source plan**
- 1B: SIPRI Yearbook plus PRC defense/CMC texts if you need direct capability or policy language.
- 2B: SIPRI military spending, Reuters for security context, and official defense statements if needed.
- 3B: Amnesty Chinese, Reuters protest coverage, and later OHCHR/HRW if you need external corroboration.
- 4B: Party Constitution, Xinhua congress texts, Reuters, and Amnesty for protest/censorship implementation.
- 5B: World Bank, IMF, and official Chinese statistical releases.
- 6B: World Bank, IMF, WHO/UNDP, and official health notices.
- 7B: For corruption-specific work, add Transparency International and CCDI/party-discipline reporting; I did not retain those here because the cross-chapter set above was tighter.
- 8B: World Bank, IMF, State Council notices, and the Xinhua congress report.

If you want, I can next turn this into a tighter chapter-by-chapter evidence dossier for 1B-8B, still without scoring.
